newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH BUILDING BOOM NOT SEEN HIT BY FIN MIN CUTS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH BUILDING BOOM NOT SEEN HIT BY FIN MIN CUTS.

text.p: Plans by the finance ministry to cut state subsidies and other funds earmarked for construction in earlier drafts of the 1998 budget make fiscal sense and will not hurt the booming sector, economists say.
The ministry's plans have led to loud protests from the construction branch and from politicians, some of whom may fear pet projects in their own constituencies could face the axe.

Finance ministry budget chief Erkki Virtanen told Reuters late last week fiscal, as well as economic and construction-specific reasons justified the plan. Activity would "not come to a halt, just slow down a bit," he said.
Esko Torsti, chief economist at SE-Banken in Helsinki, said it made sense to cut support to the heavily-subsidised construction sector now growth was in full swing.
"This is orthodox economic policy," he said.
"We are now in a quite good business cycle, also in construction," Torsti said, adding it was high time for the construction industry to start coping without state subsidies.

"If you have been receiving money for free for years you will of course scream that you are doomed if it is taken away," he said. SE-Banken forecasts housing construction growth will fall to 5-10 percent next year from 18 percent in 1997.
Economists said reports that the planned cuts were intended to prevent overheating in construction were misleading and exaggerated.
Budget chief Virtanen said the ministry had not suggested overheating, but only referred to documented bottlenecks in the supply of some construction materials.
Merita Bank economist Reijo Heiskanen said the rise in the construction costs index -- 2.5 percent yr/yr in June and 2.4 percent in May -- hardly pointed towards overheating.
"A small cut (in state support) is well justified," he said.
At Postipankki, chief economist Tarja Heinonen said protests gainst the planned cuts were probably mainly related to employment concerns.
"They are referring to employment, to the political targets," she said.

The left-right-green coalition last year vowed to increase spending on renovation construction in a drive to come closer to an elusive self-imposed target to halve the jobless rate, now at 15 percent, to 8-9 percent by the end of its term in 1999.
Heinonen called the steps planned by the finance ministry "a conditional applying of the brakes".
"I don't think it will have any significant effect on construction activity," she said, forecasting 8.7 percent growth in 1997 and 7.5 percent growth in 1998.

But at the Finnish Construction Industry Federation, director Veikko Myllyperkio said housing construction was likely to show hardly any growth in 1998 over this year if parliament ratified the planned cuts.
About 20,000 of the up-to 30,000 new apartments being built this year are built by the help of state subsidies, he said. This year's total figure compares with 23,400 in 1996.
State-subsidised housing would remain in demand due to high unemployment. People on meagre incomes cannot afford apartments built at market prices without state support, he said.

A current rise in demand for new housing at market prices was unlikely to fully compensate the sharp fall in state-subsidised building starts next year resulting from the planned cuts, Myllyperkio added.
The economists disagreed.
"Construction seems to be on a very solid trend. The momentum is quite strong," said Heiskanen at Merita.
